catalog_quote: The syllable structure of Lhaovo is: (C)V(F)/GT ... G = Glottalizedness Feature[±Glottalized] ... T = Toneme ... Lhaovo has three tonemes: Falling(F) 21; Sometimes 32 in word-initial position followed by another F; 31 after L. Low(L) 22–33; Always 22 in word-initial position followed by F; the end of the syllable rises a little bit before another L. High(H) Syllables with final stop: 44; 42 in either it has a diphtong, or it is in word-initial position. ... loF “to come back” loL “anymore” loH “to go back” ... Syllables with final stop, as well as others, show three-term opposition for tone. ... 9.1 Syllable Weakening. All syllables in Lhaovo are not “full” syllable. Some syllable are “weak” ones, that is, syllables without inherent toneme. A weak syllable depends on the syllable immediately following it, therefore it cannot appear in word/phrase final position. audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at all three locators in the held author's-PDF of Sawada 1999, a dedicated 51-pp fieldwork phonology by the language's main specialist; the paper has an obligatory Toneme slot in the syllable template, three tonemes with minimal triplets on open and checked syllables, and toneless weak syllables, and contains no stress/accent statement, so classification tonal with empty rule and domain not stated by the source is correct. Okell 1988 (downloaded now, open CC BY-SA) independently gives a 3-tone (2 on checked) system with no stress mention, and the held Sawada 2018 Lhangsu phonology likewise has tones + weak syllables and zero stress/accent hits. The only larger description (Dai 2005, Chinese, print-only) covers the PRC variety and is not expected to alter a tonal coding.

sources.citation: Okell, John A. 1988 [online ed. dated 1989]. Notes on tone alternation in Maru verbs. In D. Bradley, E.J.A. Henderson & M. Mazaudon (eds), Prosodic analysis and Asian linguistics: to honour R.K. Sprigg, 109-114. Pacific Linguistics C-104. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C104.109 (CC BY-SA online edition via sealang.net).
sources.quote: 'Tones in Maru are engagingly straightforward: there are three tones (high, mid and low) in unchecked syllables ... and two tones (high and low) in checked syllables' (p.110); the rest documents a regular morpheme-conditioned one-step tone raising in verbs. No mention of stress or accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent: 0 hits); negative/nominalizer prefixes are discussed only for their (non-)effect on tone raising.

sources.citation: Sawada, Hideo. 2018. The Phonology of Lhangsu, an Undescribed Northern-Burmish Language (北部ビルマ下位語群の未記述言語ランスー語の音韻論). In: Diversity and Dynamics of Eurasian Languages: The 20th Commemorative Volume (Contribution to the Studies of Eurasian Languages (CSEL) Series 20), 381-405. Kobe: The Consortium for the Studies of Eurasian Languages. ISBN 978-4-903875-23-1.
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog lawn1238). First-hand field description (consultant recorded 2013-2014): Lhangsu has FOUR tones - 21 (mainly with plain initials; often 31 after 22), 53 (mostly with creaky and aspirated initials), 22, and 55 (variant 35); strong pitch declination in utterances; unlike Lhaovo and Zaiwa, Lhangsu has no tonal morphemes triggering alternation on the preceding syllable; weak (toneless, reduced) syllables as in other Burmish languages (sec. 2.9). Sec. 3.3 gives tone correspondences Lhangsu: Bola: Lhaovo (F 21 / L 22 / H 44): Lacid: Zaiwa: Written Burmese, with…

tone.quote: 2.8 Tones (T) Lhangsu has four tones. Table 7 Lhangsu tones: 21 mainly with plain initials; often 31 after 22 | 53 mostly with creaky and aspirated initials | 22 | 55 with a variant 35. Drastic pitch declination was commonly observed in the speech of the consultant, even in short sentences ... This declination often makes the determination of tones fairly difficult, particularly in the case of some grammatical morphemes in clause final position. Lhaovo and Zaiwa have tonal morphemes that trigger tonal alternation to the preceding syllable (Sawada 2005, Lustig 2010), and Lacid has similar abstract morphemes that trigger vowel lengthening (Dai and Li 2007). However, Lhangsu has neither of them.
